name: Bakoko (Adie)
autonymMeaning: named after the founding ancestor Adie; linked to the name of Édéa
overview: The Adie (Bakoko) live around Édéa, mixed with the Basaa, the Bati-Mpoo and populations from elsewhere. Organised into two large families, the Benanes and the Dogtomèn, they combine fishing, hunting and farming on the banks of the Sanaga, and celebrate the Mpoo festival every year in December.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Group integrated into a varied environment: Basaa, Bati-Mpoo, Beti, Bamiléké.
Bakoko is also spoken in Logbatindi, Bela, Dibombari, Dizangué and Yakalak (Littoral).
Two families make up the group, the Benanes and the Dogtomèn. They intermarry, except when a suitor's mother comes from the other family.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The land belongs to them: they were settled there before the colonists arrived. Sanctuaries there are reserved for ceremonies of power.
Tradition has the group coming from Egypt, with stopovers at Logbikoy, in the Mfoundi, the Lékié, at Kribi and Lolodorf; good relations remain with these places.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Formerly, the eldest led the family; later heads of family, village and canton appeared.
Decisions are taken at the level of the chiefdoms, by consensus.
Social relations are free and the Adie man must respect the woman; yet a wife did not look her husband in the eye and was excluded from certain ceremonies.
Men's and women's associations, constantly renewed, regulated social life.
Relations with neighbours are good, with no inherited grudge.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; adie men readily marry women from other groups, who come to live with them.
A boy becomes a man through circumcision and by showing his skill at hunting, fishing, dancing or farming; a girl becomes a woman through physical maturity and her mastery of running the household.
Formerly, unions could be arranged very early, sometimes from the girl's birth, and abduction existed.
Steps: marriage proposal, bride price, celebration.

Bride price: kola, palm wine, jacket and machete for the father, wrapper for the mother, bottle of whisky. The kola unites the two families, the machete recalls the father's strength and work, the wrapper honours the mother's efforts, the dried cod signifies the woman's value.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: The most powerful cult is the djee, celebrated by the initiated.
Sanctuaries reserved for ancestor worship and sacred banks of the Sanaga; all rites are held in Bakoko.
Birth ensures the continuity of the group; death is merely a change of environment, the deceased remains among the living.
It is possible to get in touch with the dead for a consultation, an intercession or a request for help.
Taboos: adultery, incest, betrayal. The woman did not eat snake, a sacred meat, without her husband's consent, and did not attend burials.
Desecrating a grave or exhuming a body exposed one to expulsion, even to death.
Divination by the tarantula (mbò ngaɓi), practised by initiates.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: hunting, fishing, felling trees, farming. Women: farming, home and child-rearing, cooking.
The land went to the first arrivals and to whoever put the largest areas to productive use.
Ancestral crafts: hoes, machetes, dugout canoes, stools, drums.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Dress has moved from the loincloth to garments of bark and skins, then to the sanja, the wrapper, the shirt, the chéchia and sandals; women now wear the kaba.
Beauty: the strong, robust, hard-working man and good dancer; the woman with generous curves and well-styled hair.
Courtship: good dancer, great hunter, hard worker; for the woman, culinary art and rounded curves.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Ritual dances: the women's kòò and the djee reserved for men, as well as the bisana and the béya, performed during initiations, enthronements or the care of the sick.
Entertainment dances for rejoicing.
Instruments: tam-tam, drum, Chinese bamboo stalks.
Births, funerals and enthronements are celebrated; the Mpoo festival takes place every year in December.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: Bakoko is related to the speech varieties of other groups, such as that of the Bakoko of Etoudi (Yaoundé).

sections.title: The names
items: No strict structure; among women, ngond sometimes precedes the name.
The child receives a name linked to the circumstances of his arrival or that of a parent.
One rarely changes name, except to ward off death or bad luck.
Pseudonyms are preferred so as not to cite the father's name; the appellative replaces the prefix: Dikoume becomes à-Koum.
The founding ancestor is called Adie.

lessons.title: Who are the Bakoko (Adie)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Bakoko (Adie) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Bakoko (Adie) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Bakoko (Adie) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Bakoko (Adie) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Bakoko (Adie) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Bakoko (Adie) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Group integrated into a varied environment: Basaa, Bati-Mpoo, Beti, Bamiléké. • Bakoko is also spoken at Logbatindi, Bela, Dibombari, Dizangué and Yakalak (Littoral). • Two families make up the group, the Benanes and the Dogtomèn. They intermarry, except when a suitor's mother comes from the other family. • The land belongs to them: they were settled there before the colonists arrived. Sanctuaries there are reserved for ceremonies of power. • Tradition says the group came from Egypt, with stages at Logbikoy, in the Mfoundi, the Lékié, at Kribi and Lolodorf; good relations remain with these places.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Adie (Bakoko) live around Édéa, mixed with the Basaa, the Bati-Mpoo and populations from elsewhere. Organised into two large families, the Benanes and the Dogtomèn, they combine fishing, hunting and farming on the banks of the Sanaga, and celebrate the Mpoo festival every year in December.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Bakoko (Adie) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Bakoko (Adie)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Bakoko (Adie), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Bakoko (Adie).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Bakoko (Adie), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Bakoko (Adie).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: kona ngond, kona onde, sangàà, libod li kwèm, tega bikoyi, sugi batchengue, taro, cassava, sweet potato, macabo. • Drinks: raffia wine, palm wine. • Men: hunting, fishing, tree felling, farming. Women: farming, home and child-rearing, cooking.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Bakoko (Adie) mainly eat kona ngond, kona onde, sangàà, libod li kwèm. Traditional drinks: raffia wine, palm wine. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Bakoko (Adie)
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
lessons.competence: Explain how the Bakoko (Adie) welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Bakoko (Adie) family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Bakoko (Adie) welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Bakoko (Adie) family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • No strict structure; among women, ngond sometimes precedes the name. • The child receives a name linked to the circumstances of their arrival or that of a relative. • Names are rarely changed, except to ward off death or bad luck. • Birth ensures the group's continuity; death is only a change of environment, the deceased remains among the living. • A boy becomes a man through circumcision and by showing his skill at hunting, fishing, dancing or farming; a girl becomes a woman through physical maturity and her mastery of running a household.

steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Ritual dances: the women's kòò and the djee reserved for men, as well as the bisana and the béya, performed at initiations, enthronements or the care of the sick. • Entertainment dances for celebrations. • Instruments: tam-tam, drum, Chinese bamboo stalks. • Births, funerals and enthronements are celebrated; the Mpoo festival takes place every year in December.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Bakoko (Adie), traditional dances (kòò, djee, entertainment dances) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: tam-tam, drum, bamboos. Festival(s): December.

steps.instruction: Describe a Bakoko (Adie) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Bakoko (Adie)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bakoko (Adie), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Bakoko (Adie). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bakoko (Adie), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Bakoko (Adie). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Bakoko (Adie)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bakoko (Adie), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Bakoko (Adie). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bakoko (Adie), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Bakoko (Adie). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The most powerful cult is the djee, celebrated by the initiated. • Sanctuaries reserved for ancestor worship and the sacred banks of the Sanaga; all rites are held in Bakoko. • Birth ensures the continuity of the group; death is only a change of environment, the deceased remains among the living. • One may enter into contact with the dead for a consultation, an intercession or a request for help. • Taboos: adultery, incest, betrayal. The woman did not eat snake, a sacred meat, without her husband's consent, and did not attend burials.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The most powerful cult is the djee, celebrated by the initiated. Sanctuaries reserved for the ancestor cult and sacred banks of the Sanaga; all rites are held in Bakoko.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Bakoko (Adie) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Bakoko
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Bakoko (Adie) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Bakoko (Adie) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Bakoko (Adie) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Bakoko (Adie) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Bakoko. • Greeting formulae: Matama Mènè = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Mooni = morning greeting (one person); Ma mooni mènè = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: yaa, Bìbâa, bihàà, Binàa, Bitàan. • The founding ancestor is called Adie. • Bakoko is related to the speech varieties of other groups, such as that of the Bakoko of Etoudi (Yaoundé).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Bakoko are the first steps towards communicating with the Bakoko (Adie). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Bakoko are the first steps towards communicating with the Bakoko (Adie). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
